paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Coal is a black or brownish-black sedimentary rock that burns. It forms in layers called coal seams. It is mostly carbon, plus other elements in varying amounts, chiefly hydrogen, sulfur, oxygen and nitrogen. It is a fossil fuel: plants decay into peat, and the heat and pressure of deep burial turn that peat into coal over millions of years.

paragraphs.heading: From swamp to seam
paragraphs.text: Turning dead vegetation into coal is called coalification. At various times in the geologic past, Earth had dense forests in low-lying areas. In these wetlands the process started once dead plant matter was shielded from oxidation, usually by mud or acidic water, and turned into peat. The peat bogs trapped immense amounts of carbon and were eventually buried deep under sediments. Over millions of years, heat and pressure drove off water, methane and carbon dioxide, and the proportion of carbon rose.

paragraphs.heading: Grades of coal
paragraphs.text: The grade of coal depended on the highest pressure and temperature reached. Lignite, also called brown coal, formed under relatively mild conditions. Sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite followed in turn as temperature and pressure rose. Temperature matters much more than pressure or time of burial. Subbituminous coal can form when it is as cool as 35 to 80 °C, while anthracite needs at least 180 to 245 °C.

paragraphs.heading: Why so much formed at once
paragraphs.text: Coal is known from most geologic periods, but 90% of all coal beds were laid down in the Carboniferous and Permian periods. Paradoxically, this was a time of global glaciation, the Late Paleozoic icehouse. The glaciation came with a drop in global sea level, which exposed continental shelves that had been under water. Wide river deltas were added to these. The result was widespread wetlands with ideal conditions for coal to form.

paragraphs.heading: Wood that would not rot
paragraphs.text: Favorable geography alone does not explain the extensive coal beds of the Carboniferous. One theory suggested that some plants, about 360 million years ago, evolved the ability to make lignin, a complex polymer that made their stems much harder and more woody. That ability led to the first trees. Bacteria and fungi did not immediately evolve a way to decompose lignin, so wood did not fully decay; it was buried under sediment and eventually became coal. About 300 million years ago mushrooms and other fungi gained the ability, and the main coal-forming period ended.

paragraphs.heading: Use and cost
paragraphs.text: Coal is used mainly as a fuel. People have known and used it for thousands of years, but its use was limited until the Industrial Revolution, and consumption grew with the invention of the steam engine. In 2020 coal provided roughly a quarter of the primary energy the world used and over a third of its electricity. Extracting and burning coal damages the environment and human health, and it is the largest source of the carbon dioxide contributing to climate change. Burning coal released over fifteen billion tonnes of carbon dioxide in 2024.
